newsitem.title: USA: Ruling due in West Virginia pension case by Nov 8.
newsitem.headline: Ruling due in West Virginia pension case by Nov 8.

text.p: A judge said she would rule by Nov 8 whether West Virginia lawmakers illegally circumvented the state constitution by setting up a trust fund to invest state pension money in the stock market, state officials said.

In a hearing Thursday, Kanawha County Circuit Court Judge Lynne Ranson asked attorneys to submit written briefs on the constitutionality of the move by Oct 25. She said she would rule within two weeks of receiving them.

West Virginia's constitution prohibits equity investment of state money. In their last session, the state legislature sought to avoid the restriction by establishing an independent entity, the West Virginia Trust Fund, to receive and invest state pension and workers' compensation revenues.
Attorney General Darrell McGraw filed suit alleging that the investments could only be authorized by amending the state constitution, which would require a two-thirds voter approval.

State treasury candidate Stan Klos also filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the trust fund and another seeking to block the transfer of additional state money into the fund. The trust fund also filed a lawsuit seeking to premit the investments.

West Virginia is one of only three states that still ban equity investment of public money. The other two, South Carolina and Indiana, are scheduled to vote Nov 5 on constitutional amendments permitting the investments.

Currently West Virginia's $3.75 billion pension fund us invested in U.S. Treasuries and high-grade corporate bonds. Trust Fund executive Craig Slaughter has agreed not to buy any stocks until the litigation is resolved.
Gov. Gaston Caperton and others who support the creation of the trust fund said the move would help the state diversify and increase returns.
